steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a 3D vision paper on our method ShapeMatcher, which reconstructs objects from partial scans in arbitrary poses by retrieving and deforming database shapes. Cover the background on retrieval-and-deformation, its two main weaknesses, how our pipeline works, and a contributions list.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- 3D models from scans; applications; Retrieval and Deformation (\mathbf{R\&D})
- Two challenges of existing \mathbf{R\&D}: canonical pose assumption, partial shapes
- ShapeMatcher: joint canonicalization, segmentation, retrieval, deformation
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Background
  - surge of interest: high-quality 3D models from scans of complex scenes (cite)
  - applications: artistic creation (cite), robotics (cite), 3D scene perception (cite)
  - existing methods (cite): deep nets reconstruct directly from imperfect scans; noise + occlusion -> lose fine geometry
  - \mathbf{R\&D} techniques (cite): (1) retrieve most similar source shape from pre-curated 3D database, (2) deform it to align with target
  - good at fine details from source shapes
- Two challenges (sensitive to noise, occlusion, pose; hard to use in practice)
  - 1) most \mathbf{R\&D} methods (cite) assume target aligned in pre-processed canonical space; trained/tested on manually adjusted datasets
    - real world: manual alignment of scans or extra pose estimation networks (cite); time-intensive, laborious, inconsistent
    - blocks direct real-world use
  - 2) previous methods (cite) not designed for partially-observed shapes -> occluded objects hard
    - U-RED (cite) takes partial targets but encodes shape as one global embedding; not robust under heavy occlusion
- ShapeMatcher
  - extends \mathbf{R\&D} to joint self-supervised canonicalization, segmentation, retrieval, deformation
  - core: four associated processes trained together, supervise each other through cross-task consistency losses (Fig. 1)
  - input: partially-observed scan, arbitrary pose; four steps
  - Canonicalization: follow prior work (cite) based on Vector Neurons (cite): SE(3)-invariant point-wise features, separate translation and rotation; normalize features to remove scale (cite) -> affine-invariant features; structure disentangled from pose and size (Fig. 2 (B))
  - Segmentation: semantically consistent part segmentation + part centers (Fig. 2 (C))
  - Retrieval (Fig. 2 (D)): aggregate features per part -> retrieval token; region-weighted strategy for partial objects, weight by points inside part; robust to occlusion; compare tokens with each database shape
  - Deformation (Fig. 2 (E)): part center guided neural cage deformation (cite)
- Contributions
  - ShapeMatcher: self-supervised joint framework, partial inputs, arbitrary poses; beats state of the art by large margin on synthetic + real-world data
  - four tasks trained together, supervise each other via consistencies
  - region-weighted retrieval against occlusion

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
In recent years there has been a big increase in research interest in generating high-quality 3D models from scans of complex scenes. This technology has many applications, in artistic creation, robotics and 3D scene perception. Existing methods usually use deep neural networks directly to reconstruct 3D models from the imperfect scans. But noise and occlusions make it a big challenge to capture fine-grained geometric structures accurately. To deal with this, Retrieval and Deformation (\mathbf{R\&D}) techniques have been developed. These methods generally have two key steps. First they find the source shape that is most geometrically similar in a pre-curated 3D database, and second they deform the retrieved shape so that it aligns precisely with the target input. The \mathbf{R\&D} approach works especially well for producing 3D models with fine details that come from the source shapes.

However, existing \mathbf{R\&D} methods usually have two main challenges, which make them sensitive to noise, occlusion and pose variations and hard to use in practice. 1) Most \mathbf{R\&D} techniques assume that the target shapes are aligned in a pre-processed canonical space. These methods are usually trained and tested on datasets where the shapes were manually adjusted to this canonical state. When they are deployed in real-world settings, they need either manual alignment of the scanned objects or additional pose estimation networks. This takes a lot of time and work and can also give inconsistent results. So this limitation really gets in the way of applying these methods directly in real-world scenarios. 2) Previous methods are not specially designed for partially-observed shapes, so it is difficult for them to handle occluded objects. U-RED does take partial target shapes as input in the \mathbf{R\&D} process, but it encodes the shape directly as a global embedding, and this is not robust when there is a lot of occlusion.

- ShapeMatcher
  - extends \mathbf{R\&D} to joint self-supervised canonicalization, segmentation, retrieval, deformation; cross-task consistency losses (Fig. 1)
  - Canonicalization: SE(3)-invariant features (Vector Neurons), scale normalization -> affine-invariant (Fig. 2 (B))
  - Segmentation: part segmentation + part centers (Fig. 2 (C))
  - Retrieval: per-part features -> retrieval token, region-weighted for partial objects (Fig. 2 (D))
  - Deformation: part center guided neural cage deformation (Fig. 2 (E))
- Contributions
  - joint self-supervised framework, partial inputs, arbitrary poses; large margin on synthetic + real data
  - four tasks supervise each other via consistencies
  - region-weighted retrieval against occlusion

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
In recent years there has been a big increase in research interest in generating high-quality 3D models from scans of complex scenes. This technology has many applications, in artistic creation, robotics and 3D scene perception. Existing methods usually use deep neural networks directly to reconstruct 3D models from the imperfect scans. But noise and occlusions make it a big challenge to capture fine-grained geometric structures accurately. To deal with this, Retrieval and Deformation (\mathbf{R\&D}) techniques have been developed. These methods generally have two key steps. First they find the source shape that is most geometrically similar in a pre-curated 3D database, and second they deform the retrieved shape so that it aligns precisely with the target input. The \mathbf{R\&D} approach works especially well for producing 3D models with fine details that come from the source shapes.

However, existing \mathbf{R\&D} methods usually have two main challenges, which make them sensitive to noise, occlusion and pose variations and hard to use in practice. 1) Most \mathbf{R\&D} techniques assume that the target shapes are aligned in a pre-processed canonical space. These methods are usually trained and tested on datasets where the shapes were manually adjusted to this canonical state. When they are deployed in real-world settings, they need either manual alignment of the scanned objects or additional pose estimation networks. This takes a lot of time and work and can also give inconsistent results. So this limitation really gets in the way of applying these methods directly in real-world scenarios. 2) Previous methods are not specially designed for partially-observed shapes, so it is difficult for them to handle occluded objects. U-RED does take partial target shapes as input in the \mathbf{R\&D} process, but it encodes the shape directly as a global embedding, and this is not robust when there is a lot of occlusion.

To address these two challenges, in this paper we present ShapeMatcher, a new framework that extends the traditional \mathbf{R\&D} pipeline to joint self-supervised learning of object canonicalization, segmentation, retrieval and deformation. Our core contribution is that the four processes are highly associated, so they can be trained at the same time and supervise each other through several cross-task consistency losses (Fig. 1). Given a partially-observed object scan in an arbitrary pose, ShapeMatcher processes the object in four steps. First, we follow prior work, which is based on Vector Neurons, to extract SE(3)-invariant point-wise features by separating translation and rotation progressively. We also follow another work to normalize the features so that the object scale is disassociated. At this point we have affine-invariant point-wise features, since the object's inherent structure is disentangled from its pose and size. This makes it possible to do Canonicalization of the observed object based on these intrinsic characteristics (Fig. 2 (B)). Next we feed the learned features into our Segmentation module (Fig. 2 (C)) to predict semantically consistent part segmentation and the corresponding part centers. Then in the Retrieval module (Fig. 2 (D)), based on the part segmentation, we aggregate features inside each part and put them together as a comprehensive retrieval token for the object. For partial objects we introduce a region-weighted strategy, where each part gets a weight according to the points inside it. Parts with more points get higher weights in retrieval, and this is shown to be robust to occlusions. We compare the tokens of the target object with each shape in the pre-constructed database to find the most geometrically similar source shape (the one with the most similar tokens). Finally, in the Deformation module (Fig. 2 (E)), the retrieved source shape is deformed to tightly match the target object using part center guided neural cage deformation.

Our main contributions are:

- We introduce ShapeMatcher, a new self-supervised framework for joint shape canonicalization, segmentation, retrieval and deformation, which handles partial target inputs under arbitrary poses. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show that ShapeMatcher is better than existing state-of-the-art approaches by a large margin.

- We show that the four highly-associated tasks, canonicalization, segmentation, retrieval and deformation, can be trained together effectively and supervise each other by constructing consistencies.

- We develop the region-weighted retrieval method to reduce the impact of occlusions in the \mathbf{R\&D} process.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
In recent years, there has been a notable increase in research interest in generating high-quality 3D models from scans of complex scenes [1,2,3,4,5,6,7]. This technology enables extensive applications in artistic creation [8,9], robotics [10,11] and 3D scene perception [12,13]. Existing methods [14,12] typically use deep neural networks to directly reconstruct 3D models from imperfect scans. However, noise and occlusions make it challenging to accurately capture fine-grained geometric structures. To overcome this, Retrieval and Deformation (\mathbf{R\&D}) techniques [15,9,16,8,17,18,19,20] have been developed. These methods generally involve two key steps: first, identifying the most geometrically similar source shape from a pre-curated 3D database; and second, deforming the retrieved shape to align precisely with the target input. The \mathbf{R\&D} approach is particularly effective at producing 3D models enriched with fine details from the source shapes.

However, existing \mathbf{R\&D} methods usually face two primary challenges that make them susceptible to noise, occlusion and pose variations, and difficult to use in practice. 1) Most \mathbf{R\&D} techniques [15,9,16,8,17,18,19,20,21] assume that target shapes are aligned in a pre-processed canonical space. Typically, these methods are trained and tested on datasets where shapes have been manually adjusted to this canonical state. When deployed in real-world settings, they therefore require either manual alignment of scanned objects or additional pose estimation networks [22,23,24,25,26]. Such procedures are time-intensive and laborious, and they are also prone to inconsistent results. This limitation significantly impedes the direct application of these methods in real-world scenarios. 2) Previous methods [9,8] are not specially designed for partially-observed shapes, which makes it difficult to handle occluded objects. Although U-RED [21] takes partial target shapes as input in the \mathbf{R\&D} process, it directly encodes the shape as a global embedding, which is not robust under significant occlusion.

To address these two challenges, in this paper we present ShapeMatcher, a novel framework that extends the traditional \mathbf{R\&D} pipeline to joint self-supervised learning of object canonicalization, segmentation, retrieval and deformation. Our core contribution is that the four highly-associated processes can be trained simultaneously and supervise each other through several cross-task consistency losses (Fig. 1). Specifically, given a partially-observed object scan in an arbitrary pose, ShapeMatcher processes the object in four steps. First, we follow [27], which is based on Vector Neurons [28], to extract SE(3)-invariant point-wise features by progressively separating translation and rotation. We further follow [29] to normalize the features and disassociate the object scale. We thus obtain affine-invariant point-wise features by disentangling the object's inherent structure from its pose and size, which facilitates the Canonicalization of the observed object based on these intrinsic characteristics (Fig. 2 (B)). Then we predict semantically consistent part segmentation and the corresponding part centers by feeding the learned features into our Segmentation module (Fig. 2 (C)). Based on the part segmentation, the Retrieval module (Fig. 2 (D)) aggregates features within each part and collects them into a comprehensive retrieval token of the object. For partial objects, we introduce a region-weighted strategy that assigns each part a weight according to the points inside it. Parts with more points receive higher weights during retrieval, which proves robust to occlusions. We compare the tokens of the target object with each shape in the pre-constructed database to identify the most geometrically similar source shape. In the final Deformation module (Fig. 2 (E)), the retrieved source shape is deformed to tightly match the target object via part center guided neural cage deformation [17].

To summarize, our main contributions are:

- We introduce ShapeMatcher, a novel self-supervised framework for joint shape canonicalization, segmentation, retrieval and deformation that handles partial target inputs under arbitrary poses. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that ShapeMatcher surpasses existing state-of-the-art approaches by a large margin.

- We demonstrate that the four highly-associated tasks, canonicalization, segmentation, retrieval and deformation, can be effectively trained simultaneously and supervise each other by constructing consistencies.

- We develop the region-weighted retrieval method to mitigate the impact of occlusions in the \mathbf{R\&D} process.
